21       On August 9, 2024, Procopio, Cory, Hargreaves & Savitch, LLP and associates 
22  Sean M. Sullivan and Justin M. Martin (“Counsel”) filed an ex parte motion to withdraw 
23  as counsel for Plaintiff Aaron Stanz (“Plaintiff”).  ECF No. 131.  By the Court’s order, 
24  Plaintiff filed a response.  ECF No. 141.                                 
25       Counsel moved to withdraw as counsel on the grounds that Plaintiff has not met 
26  the material terms of the engagement agreement and that there are now irreconcilable 
27                                                                            
1  differences.  ECF No. 131.  The ABA’s Model Rules of Professional Conduct1 permit a 
2  lawyer to withdrawal as counsel if the client renders it unreasonably difficult for the 
3  lawyer to carry out the representation effectively, Model Rules of Prof. Conduct R. 
4  1.16(b)(6), or when the client breaches a material term of an agreement with the lawyer, 
5  and the lawyer has given reasonable warning after the breach that the lawyer will 
6  withdraw unless the client fulfills the obligation, Model Rules of Prof. Conduct. R. 
7  1.16(b)(5).                                                               
8       On September 17, Counsel and Plaintiff conferred by telephone and discussed 
9  these two grounds for withdrawal.  ECF No. 143.  The parties could not reach an 
10  agreement that these issues could be resolved.  Id.                       
11       After consideration of the papers submitted, the results of the September 17 
12  meeting between Counsel and Plaintiff, and the September 20 hearing with Counsel, 
13  Plaintiff, and defense counsel present, the Court finds that voluntary withdrawal is 
14  warranted and GRANTS the Counsel’s motion to withdraw.                    
15       Moreover, it does not appear that Counsel’s withdrawal would unduly prejudice 
16  the parties, harm the administration of justice, or unduly delay the resolution of this case.  
17  See In re Saber, No. 21-55913, 2022 WL 11592836, at *1 (9th Cir. Oct. 20, 2022).  A 
18  Final Pretrial Conference is set for March 7, 2025.  Given this date, there is sufficient 
19  time for new counsel to be hired and then familiarized with the case without unduly 
20  delaying proceedings or prejudicing Plaintiff.  Cf. In re Saber, 2022 WL 11592836, at *1

21       On December 12, 2024, Higgs Fletcher & Mack, LLP and all attorneys associated 
22  with it including Nicholas D. Brauns and Edwin M. Boniske (“Movant”) filed an ex parte 
23  motion to withdraw from representation of Defendants Jordan Brown, Jet Genius 
24  Holdings, Inc., Jet Genius Florida Holdings, Inc., C3 Jets LLC, C3 Limo LLC, Jet 
25  Agency Global, LLC, and Bowman Aviation, Inc. (“Defendants”) and to substitute 
26  Defendant Jordan Brown pro se.  ECF No. 179 (“Mot.”). For the reasons set forth below, 
27                                                                            
1  the Court GRANTS the motion to withdraw and ORDERS that corporate Defendants 
2  obtain new counsel within 45 days of the filling of this Order.           
3                              BACKGROUND                                    
4       On December 12, 2024, Counsel moved to withdraw as counsel on the grounds 
5  that Defendants have not met the material terms of the engagement agreement by which 
6  they engaged Movant for legal services.  ECF No. 179.  According to Movant, good 
7  cause for withdrawal exists because Defendants have failed to pay their legal fees.  Id.  
8  Furthermore, Movant states that the withdrawal would not prejudice the other litigants, 
9  the administration of justice, or the resolution of the case because the case is still in 
10  discovery.  See Mot. at 6, Brauns Decl. ¶ 4 (attesting that, at that point in time, no 
11  depositions have taken place or are even scheduled).                      
12       Movant advised Defendants and Plaintiff’s Counsel that it would be making an ex 
13  parte request to withdraw as counsel for Defendants, thereby complying with Civ.L.R. 
14  83.3(g)(2), see Mot. at 5, Brauns Decl. ¶ 7.  Movant also notified the business-entity 
15  defendants that they cannot proceed without counsel in this action.  Mot., Brauns Decl. ¶ 
16  5.  Neither Plaintiff nor Defendants have opposed this request.           
17       On January 7, 2025, the Court directed Defendants to file, within a week, a 
18  response to the motion to withdraw.  ECF No. 186.  Defendants never responded.  On 
19  January 17, 2025, Mr. Brauns filed a declaration attesting that he forwarded the Court’s 
20  Order to Defendants and that he reminded Defendants twice of the Order via email.  ECF 
21  No. 194.                                                                  
22                            LEGAL STANDARD                                  
23       “An attorney may not withdraw as counsel except by leave of court, and the 
24  decision to grant or deny counsel's motion to withdraw is committed to the discretion of 
25  the trial court.”  Beard v. Shuttermart of Cal., Inc., No. 07–CV–594–WQH (NLS), 2008 
26  WL 410694, at *2 (S.D.Cal. Feb.13, 2008) (internal quotation marks and citations 
27                                                                            
1  omitted); see also Civ. L.R. 83.3(g)(3).  In ruling on a motion to withdraw as counsel, 
2  courts consider: (1) the reasons why withdrawal is sought; (2) the prejudice withdrawal 
3  may cause to other litigants; (3) the harm withdrawal might cause to the administration of 
4  justice; and (4) the degree to which withdrawal will delay the resolution of the 
5  case.  Beard, 2008 WL 410694, at *2 (citations omitted).                  
6       The ABA’s Model Rules of Professional Conduct1 permit a lawyer to withdrawal 
7  as counsel if the client breaches a material term of an agreement with the lawyer, and the 
8  lawyer has given reasonable warning after the breach that the lawyer will withdraw 
9  unless the client fulfills the obligation, Model Rules of Prof. Conduct. R. 1.16(b)(5).  
10                               DISCUSSION                                   
11       The Court finds that good cause exists to grant the motion to withdraw as counsel.  
12  “Failure to pay attorney's fees can be a valid ground for withdrawal.”  Leatt Corp. v. 
13  Inn've Safety Tech., LLC, No. 09-CV-1301, 2010 WL 444708, at *2 (S.D. Cal, Feb. 2, 
14  2010); see Model Rules of Prof. Conduct R. 1.16(b)(5).  Movant has given Defendants 
15  sufficient notice that it would withdraw from representation unless Defendants fulfilled 
16  their obligations under the engagement agreement.  See Mot. at 5, Brauns Decl. ¶ 3. 
17       Furthermore, it does not appear that Counsel’s withdrawal would unduly prejudice 
18  the parties, harm the administration of justice, or unduly delay the resolution of this case.  
19  See In re Saber, No. 21-55913, 2022 WL 11592836, at *1 (9th Cir. Oct. 20, 2022).  A 
20  Final Pretrial Conference is set for June 27, 2025.  See ECF No. 138.  Given this date,

   standards of professional conduct required by the State Bar of California.  See generally

24       Before the Court is Plaintiff Aaron Stanz’s (“Plaintiff” or “Stanz”) Motion for 
25  Leave to File a First Amended Complaint. ECF No. 16. Defendants Jordan Brown 
26  (“Brown”); C3jets LLC (“C3jets”); and Jet Genius Florida Holdings, Inc. (“JGFH”) filed 
27  Oppositions. ECF Nos. 19, 20. Plaintiff filed Replies to both Oppositions. ECF Nos. 22, 
28  23.  Based on the reasoning below, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to 
1  File a First Amended Complaint. Plaintiff shall file an amended complaint within five (5) 
2  days of the Court’s order.  The hearing currently set for March 3, 2023 is VACATED.  
3                              BACKGROUND                                    
4       On August 8, 2022, Plaintiff filed a Complaint against Defendants Jordan Brown; 
5  Jet Genius Holdings, Inc.; Jet Genius Florida Holdings, Inc.; C3jets LLC; and Bowman 
6  Aviation LLC (collectively “Defendants”) alleging numerous causes of action for: (1) 
7  violations of the Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1); (2) violation of the 
8  California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, Cal. Civ. Code § 3426; (3) breach of contract; (4) 
9  breach of fiduciary duty; (5) fraud; (6) conspiracy; (7) accounting; and (8) unjust 
10  enrichment. ECF No. 1 (Compl.) ¶¶ 51-141. Plaintiff’s initial Complaint presents 
11  numerous factual allegations, including that Defendant Brown “misappropriated 
12  Plaintiff’s (and his company’s) intellectual property and set up new companies to evade 
13  the FET [Federal Excise Tax] and dilute Plaintiff’s shareholder value.” Id. ¶ 2.  
14       On September 9, 2022, Defendants Brown and C3jets filed a Motion to Dismiss. 
15  ECF No. 3. Plaintiff did not respond to the Motion, and instead filed an Amended 
16  Complaint on October 11, 2022. ECF No. 6. Because Plaintiff’s First Amended 
17  Complaint (“FAC”) was filed more than 21 days after service of Defendants’ Motion to 
18  Dismiss, (Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1)(B)), the Court struck the Amended Complaint as 
19  untimely under Rule 15(a)(1). ECF No. 19.                                 
20       On December 5, 2022, Defendant Jet Genius Holdings, Inc. (“JGH”) filed a 
21  Motion to Dismiss. ECF No. 11. On December 6, 2022, Defendant JGFH filed a Motion 
22  to Dismiss. ECF No. 12. On December 27, 2022, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Leave to 
23  Amend the Complaint. ECF No. 16. The Court set a briefing schedule and vacated the 
24  hearing on the Motions to Dismiss pending the Court’s ruling on the instant Motion. ECF 
25  No. 17. On January 25, 2023, Defendants Jordan Brown, C3jets, and JGFH filed 
26  Oppositions to Plaintiff’s Motion. ECF Nos. 19, 20. On February 8, 2023, Plaintiff filed 
27  his Replies. ECF Nos. 22, 23.                                             
28                                                                            
1       The Proposed First Amended Complaint (“PFAC”) is substantially different from 
2  the initial Complaint. See ECF No. 16-5; ECF No. 21-1 (redline version). The PFAC 
3  appears to add factual allegations, parties, and causes of action. Plaintiff states that 
4  “[s]ince filing his original complaint, [he] has discovered new information” and now 
5  seeks to add three new Defendants—C3 Limo LLC, Jet Agency Global LLC, and the 
6  Brown Family Trust1—as well as additional causes of action “under RICO and for 
7  Equitable Contribution.” ECF No. 16-1 at 1, 3. Defendants Brown, C3jets, and JGFH 
8  oppose Plaintiff’s Motion primarily on the grounds that the PFAC does not 
9  “meaningfully address the legal issues raised in Defendants’ pending Motions to Dismiss 
10  and Strike” and because the new causes of action fail to state a claim for relief. ECF No. 
11  19 at 6-7; see also ECF No. 20 at 8.                                      
12                     REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE                            
13       As a preliminary matter, the Court grants Defendants’ request for judicial notice of 
14  Plaintiff’s initial Complaint, (ECF No. 1), Defendants Jordan Brown and C3jets’s Motion 
15  to Dismiss and supporting documents, (ECF No. 3), and Defendant JGFH’s Motion to 
16  Dismiss, (ECF No. 12). See Harris v. Cnty. of Orange, 682 F.3d 1126, 1132 (9th Cir. 
17  2012) (“We may take judicial notice of undisputed matters of public record, including 
18  documents on file in federal or state courts.”). Because Defendants request notice of 
19  documents filed in this Court, and Plaintiff has not opposed this request, the Court 
20  GRANTS Defendants’ requests for judicial notice. See ECF No. 19-1, 20-2.  
21                            LEGAL STANDARD                                  
22       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“Rule”) 15(a), “[a] party may amend its 
23  pleading once as a matter of course within (A) 21 days after serving it; or (B) 21 days 
24  after service of a motion under Rule 12(b) . . . .” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1). “In all other 
25                                                                            

26                                                                            
27  1 Defendants’ Opposition argues that a family trust cannot be sued. See ECF No. 19 at 17. 
   Plaintiff concedes this and states that he “will remove the Family trust as a defendant.” 
28                                                                            
1  cases, a party may amend its pleading only with the opposing party’s written consent or 
2  the court’s leave,” and courts “should freely give leave when justice so requires.”  Fed. R. 
3  Civ. P. 15(a)(2); see also Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962) (“Rule 15(a) 
4  declares that leave to amend ‘shall be freely given when justice so requires’; this mandate 
5  is to be heeded.”); DCD Programs, Ltd. v. Leighton, 833 F.2d 183, 186 (9th Cir. 1987) 
6  (stating “[R]ule 15’s policy of favoring amendments to pleadings should be applied with 
7  ‘extreme liberality’”).                                                   
8       In assessing the propriety of an amendment, courts consider several factors: (1) 
9  undue delay; (2) bad faith or dilatory motive; (3) repeated failure to cure deficiencies by 
10  amendments previously permitted;2 (4) prejudice to the opposing party; and (5) futility of 
11  amendment.  Foman, 371 U.S. at 182; United States v. Corinthian Colleges, 655 F.3d 
12  984, 995 (9th Cir. 2011). These factors do not carry equal weight; the possibility of delay 
13  alone, for instance, cannot justify denial of leave to amend. DCD Programs, 833 F.2d at 
14  186. The single most important factor is whether prejudice would result to the non-
15  movant as a consequence of the amendment. Eminence Cap., LLC v. Aspeon, Inc., 316 
16  F.3d 1048, 1052 (9th Cir. 2003) (“As this circuit and others have held, it is the 
17  consideration of prejudice to the opposing party that carries the greatest weight.”). The 
18  burden of demonstrating prejudice falls on the party opposing leave to amend. DCD 
19  Programs, 833 F.2d at 187.                                                
20       When determining whether to grant leave to amend, courts must bear in mind that 
21  “the underlying purpose of Rule 15 [is] to facilitate decisions on the merits, rather than on 
22  the pleadings or technicalities.”  Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1127 (9th Cir. 2000) (en 
23  banc); see also In re Zoom Video Commc’ns Inc. Priv. Litig., 525 F. Supp. 32 1017, 1027 
24  (N.D. Cal. 2021).                                                         
25                                                                            
26                                                                            

27                                                                            
   2 Because this is Plaintiff’s first amended complaint, the Court does not discuss this 
28                                                                            
1                                 DISCUSSION                                 
2       A.   Undue Delay                                                     
3       First, the Court must determine if Plaintiff unduly delayed in filing this Motion. 
4  “Relevant to evaluating the delay issue is whether the moving party knew or should have 
5  known the facts and theories raised by the amendment in the original pleading.” Jackson 
6  v. Bank of Hawaii, 902 F.2d 1385, 1389 (9th Cir. 1990). A court should also determine if 
7  “permitting amendment would . . . produce an undue delay in the litigation.” Waryck v. 
8  Thor Motor Coach Inc., 2023 WL 300138, at *2 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 18, 2023) (quoting 
9  Jackson, 902 F.2d at 1387).                                               
10       Plaintiff argues that there is no undue delay and amendment will not alter the 
11  proceeding’s scheduling. ECF No. 16-1 at 8. Plaintiff states the case has only been active 
12  for 4.5 months and there is “sufficient time remaining for the parties to conduct relevant 
13  discovery.” Id. Neither Opposition argues undue delay is present.         
14       The Court finds Plaintiff has not unduly delayed. A Declaration submitted by 
15  Plaintiff’s counsel Wade Miller states that, following filing the initial Complaint, “new 
16  and important facts continue[] to come to light.” ECF No. 16-2 ¶ 9. Plaintiff alleges he 
17  “has discovered new information regarding Defendants, and these new details support 
18  Plaintiff’s previously asserted claims.” ECF No. 16-1 at 7. Specifically, following filing 
19  of the initial Complaint, Plaintiff and counsel were “made aware of actions by Defendant 
20  Jordan Brown against his business competitor, Jason Johnson.” Id. at 5. Plaintiff states he 
21  learned Defendant Brown made threats to kill Johnson and argues that this discovery 
22  supports the addition of a RICO cause of action, because RICO “includes ‘any act or 
23  threat involving murder.’” Id. at 7 (citing 18 U.S.C. § 1961(1)(A)). In addition, because 
24  this Motion to Amend was filed only 4.5 months after the initial Complaint, the Court 
25  finds amendment at this stage will not substantially delay litigation. See also Waryck, 
26  2023 WL 300138 at *2 (finding no undue delay when motion for amendment was filed 
27  three months after commencement of the action because it was an “early stage of 
28  proceedings”). No scheduling order has been issued, and discovery has not yet begun. See 
1  also SAES Getters S.p.A. v. Aeronex, Inc., 219 F. Supp. 2d 1081 (S.D. Cal. 2002) (“To 
2  show undue delay, the opposing party must at least show delay past the point of initiation 
3  of discovery . . . .”). Thus, this factor weighs in favor of granting leave to amend. 
4       B.   Bad Faith                                                       
5       Bad faith exists when the proposed amendment “will not save the complaint or the 
6  plaintiff merely is seeking to prolong the litigation by adding new but baseless legal 
7  theories.” Griggs v. Pace Am. Grp., Inc., 170 F.3d 877, 881 (9th Cir. 1999). Bad faith 
8  may also be present when the moving party has a “‘history of dilatory tactics.’” Naranjo 
9  v. Bank of Am. Nat’l Ass’n, 2015 WL 913031, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 27, 2015) (quoting 
10  Thornton v. McClatchy Newspapers, Inc., 261 F.3d 789, 799 (9th Cir. 2001)). A court 
11  should look to the record to determine if bad faith exists. Id. (citing DCD Programs, 833 
12  F.2d at 187).                                                             
13       Plaintiff argues there is no evidence of bad faith. Defendants do not make any 
14  argument Plaintiff is acting in bad faith. The Court agrees. Plaintiff does not appear to be 
15  attempting to prolong the litigation. As stated above, the initial Complaint was filed only 
16  four and a half months prior to the present Motion, and discovery has not yet started. 
17  Thus, this factor weighs in favor of granting leave.                      
18       C.   Prejudice                                                       
19       “Prejudice is the touchstone of the inquiry under Rule 15(a),” and “[a]bsent 
20  prejudice, or a strong showing of any of the remaining Foman factors, there exists a 
21  presumption under Rule 15(a) in favor of granting a leave to amend.”  Eminence Cap., 
22  316 F.3d at1052 (internal quotations omitted). Prejudice may exist where new allegations 
23  “greatly alter[] the nature of the litigation” and would require defendants to undertake, “at 
24  a late hour, an entirely new course of defense.” Morongo Band of Mission Indians v. 
25  Rose, 893 F.2d 1074, 1079 (9th Cir. 1990); Peterson v. California, No. 1:10-cv-01132-
26  SMS, 2011 WL 3875622, at *3 (E.D. Cal. Sept. 1, 2011) (“[W]hen, after a period of 
27  extensive discovery, a party proposes a late-tendered amendment that would 
28  fundamentally change the case to incorporate new causes of action and that would require 
1  additional discovery, the amendment may be appropriately denied as prejudicial to the 
2  opposing party.”).                                                        
3       Here, Defendants make no argument they will suffer from undue prejudice should 
4  Plaintiff’s Motion to Amend be granted, and as stated above, it is the non-movant’s 
5  burden to demonstrate prejudice. Plaintiff argues that he does “not add these parties or 
6  new claims late to litigation as the case was only filed in August of 2022.” ECF No. 16-1 
7  at 9.                                                                     
8       The Court finds amendment at this stage and under these circumstances would not 
9  unduly prejudice Defendants. The new claims and allegations do not alter the nature of 
10  the litigation to a significant extent as they all concern Defendant Brown’s allegedly 
11  improper and illegal actions. Further, the litigation is in early stages.  Plaintiff filed his 
12  Motion for Leave to Amend only four and a half months after filing of the initial 
13  Complaint. Defendants have filed Motions to Dismiss, but no significant briefing has 
14  occurred on the arguments presented therein. See Fremantlemedia N. Am., Inc. v. AXA 
15  Ins. Co., 2010 WL 11601204, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Nov. 5, 2010) (granting motion for leave 
16  to amend because the case was in “its early stages and neither party has conducted 
17  discovery, except for initial disclosures”). Accordingly, Defendant has not demonstrated 
18  it would be prejudiced by the filing of an amended complaint, and thus, this factor weighs 
19  in favor of granting leave to amend.                                      
20       D.   Futility                                                        
21       An amendment is futile “only if it would clearly be subject to dismissal.” SAES 
22  Getters, 219 F. Supp. 2d at 1086 (citing DCD Programs, 83 F.2d at 188). Amendment is 
23  futile when a court could not “conceive of additional facts that could, if formally alleged, 
24  support the claim[s].” Corinthian Colls., 655 F.3d at 995. “While courts will determine 
25  the legal sufficiency of a proposed amendment using the same standard as applied on a 
26  Rule 12(b)(6) motion . . . such issues are often more appropriately raised in a motion to 
27  dismiss rather than in an opposition to a motion for leave to amend.” SAES Getters, 219 
28  F. Supp. 2d at 1086. Courts generally do not consider the validity of a proposed amended 
1 || pleading in deciding whether to grant leave to amend, instead deferring consideration of 
2    challenges to the merits after leave to amend is granted and the amended pleadings are 
3 || filed. See id.; Clarke v.  Upton, 703 F. Supp. 2d 1037,  1043 (E.D. Cal. 2010) (“[D]enial 
4        a motion to amend] on this ground is rare and courts generally defer considerations of 
5 || challenges to the merits of a proposed amended pleading until after leave to amend is 
6 || granted and the amended pleading 1s filed.’’). 
7         Due to the complexity of the legal issues and sheer volume of factual allegations, 
8 || arguments, and Defendants, the Court finds Defendants’ arguments are more 
9 || appropriately resolved at the Motion to Dismiss stage after substantive briefing by all 
10 || Parties. Plaintiff has yet to respond to the Motions to Dismiss and was limited to the 
11    length of a Reply brief to respond to Defendants’ substantive arguments presented in 
12 || their Oppositions to the present Motion. Due to the complicated nature of the factual 
13 || allegations and causes of action, the Court is not prepared to say that there exists no 
14 || factual scenario in which all or some of Plaintiff's causes of action can survive a Motion 
15        Dismiss against all or some of the Defendants. 
16         Overall, the Foman factors weigh in favor of permitting Plaintiff to amend his 
17   ||Complaint. The Court GRANTS Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to File an Amended 
18   ||Complaint given the strong federal policy favoring amendments due to a preference for 
19 || resolving cases on the merits. See DCD Programs, Ltd., 833 F.2d at 186. 
20                                     CONCLUSION 
21         For the reasons set forth above, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff's Motion for Leave 
22       File an Amended Complaint.  Plaintiff shall file an Amended Complaint within five (5) 
23 || days of the Court’s order. The hearing currently set for March 3, 2023 is VACATED. 
24 || The pending Motions to Dismiss are DENIED as MOOT. 
25         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
26    Dated:  February 27, 2023                 2
27                                           Hon. athe Cae 
28                                           United States District Judge

21                            LEGAL STANDARD                                  
22       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“Rule”) 15(a), “[a] party may amend its 
23  pleading once as a matter of course within (A) 21 days after serving it; or (B) 21 days 
24  after service of a motion under Rule 12(b) . . . .” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1). “In all other

1  cases, a party may amend its pleading only with the opposing party’s written consent or 
2  the court’s leave,” and courts “should freely give leave when justice so requires.”  Fed. R. 
3  Civ. P. 15(a)(2); see also Foman v. Davis,
371 U.S. 178, 182
 (1962) (“Rule 15(a) 
4  declares that leave to amend ‘shall be freely given when justice so requires’; this mandate 
5  is to be heeded.”); DCD Programs, Ltd. v. Leighton,
833 F.2d 183, 186
 (9th Cir. 1987) 
6  (stating “[R]ule 15’s policy of favoring amendments to pleadings should be applied with 
7  ‘extreme liberality’”).                                                   
8       In assessing the propriety of an amendment, courts consider several factors: (1) 
9  undue delay; (2) bad faith or dilatory motive; (3) repeated failure to cure deficiencies by 
10  amendments previously permitted;2 (4) prejudice to the opposing party; and (5) futility of 
11  amendment.  Foman,
371 U.S. at 182
; United States v. Corinthian Colleges,
655 F.3d 12 984, 995
 (9th Cir. 2011). These factors do not carry equal weight; the possibility of delay 
13  alone, for instance, cannot justify denial of leave to amend. DCD Programs,
833 F.2d at 14
  186. The single most important factor is whether prejudice would result to the non-
15  movant as a consequence of the amendment. Eminence Cap., LLC v. Aspeon, Inc., 316
16 F.3d 1048, 1052
 (9th Cir. 2003) (“As this circuit and others have held, it is the 
17  consideration of prejudice to the opposing party that carries the greatest weight.”). The 
18  burden of demonstrating prejudice falls on the party opposing leave to amend. DCD 
19  Programs,
833 F.2d at 187
.                                                
20       When determining whether to grant leave to amend, courts must bear in mind that 
21  “the underlying purpose of Rule 15 [is] to facilitate decisions on the merits, rather than on 
22  the pleadings or technicalities.”  Lopez v. Smith,
203 F.3d 1122, 1127
 (9th Cir. 2000) (en 
23  banc); see also In re Zoom Video Commc’ns Inc. Priv. Litig.,
525 F. Supp. 32
 1017, 1027 
24  (N.D. Cal. 2021).

2       A.   Undue Delay                                                     
3       First, the Court must determine if Plaintiff unduly delayed in filing this Motion. 
4  “Relevant to evaluating the delay issue is whether the moving party knew or should have 
5  known the facts and theories raised by the amendment in the original pleading.” Jackson 
6  v. Bank of Hawaii,
902 F.2d 1385, 1389
 (9th Cir. 1990). A court should also determine if 
7  “permitting amendment would . . . produce an undue delay in the litigation.” Waryck v. 
8  Thor Motor Coach Inc.,
2023 WL 300138
, at *2 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 18, 2023) (quoting 
9  Jackson,
902 F.2d at 1387
).                                               
10       Plaintiff argues that there is no undue delay and amendment will not alter the 
11  proceeding’s scheduling. ECF No. 16-1 at 8. Plaintiff states the case has only been active 
12  for 4.5 months and there is “sufficient time remaining for the parties to conduct relevant 
13  discovery.”
Id.
 Neither Opposition argues undue delay is present.         
14       The Court finds Plaintiff has not unduly delayed. A Declaration submitted by 
15  Plaintiff’s counsel Wade Miller states that, following filing the initial Complaint, “new 
16  and important facts continue[] to come to light.” ECF No. 16-2 ¶ 9. Plaintiff alleges he 
17  “has discovered new information regarding Defendants, and these new details support

19  of the initial Complaint, Plaintiff and counsel were “made aware of actions by Defendant

21  learned Defendant Brown made threats to kill Johnson and argues that this discovery 
22  supports the addition of a RICO cause of action, because RICO “includes ‘any act or 
23  threat involving murder.’” Id. at 7 (citing
18 U.S.C. § 1961
(1)(A)). In addition, because 
24  this Motion to Amend was filed only 4.5 months after the initial Complaint, the Court 
25  finds amendment at this stage will not substantially delay litigation. See also Waryck, 
26
2023 WL 300138
 at *2 (finding no undue delay when motion for amendment was filed 
27  three months after commencement of the action because it was an “early stage of 
28  proceedings”). No scheduling order has been issued, and discovery has not yet begun. See 
1  also SAES Getters S.p.A. v. Aeronex, Inc.,
219 F. Supp. 2d 1081
 (S.D. Cal. 2002) (“To 
2  show undue delay, the opposing party must at least show delay past the point of initiation 
3  of discovery . . . .”). Thus, this factor weighs in favor of granting leave to amend. 
4       B.   Bad Faith                                                       
5       Bad faith exists when the proposed amendment “will not save the complaint or the 
6  plaintiff merely is seeking to prolong the litigation by adding new but baseless legal 
7  theories.” Griggs v. Pace Am. Grp., Inc.,
170 F.3d 877
, 881 (9th Cir. 1999). Bad faith 
8  may also be present when the moving party has a “‘history of dilatory tactics.’” Naranjo 
9  v. Bank of Am. Nat’l Ass’n,
2015 WL 913031
, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 27, 2015) (quoting 
10  Thornton v. McClatchy Newspapers, Inc.,
261 F.3d 789, 799
 (9th Cir. 2001)). A court 
11  should look to the record to determine if bad faith exists.
Id.
 (citing DCD Programs, 833 
12  F.2d at 187).                                                             
13       Plaintiff argues there is no evidence of bad faith. Defendants do not make any 
14  argument Plaintiff is acting in bad faith. The Court agrees. Plaintiff does not appear to be 
15  attempting to prolong the litigation. As stated above, the initial Complaint was filed only 
16  four and a half months prior to the present Motion, and discovery has not yet started. 
17  Thus, this factor weighs in favor of granting leave.                      
18       C.   Prejudice                                                       
19       “Prejudice is the touchstone of the inquiry under Rule 15(a),” and “[a]bsent 
20  prejudice, or a strong showing of any of the remaining Foman factors, there exists a 
21  presumption under Rule 15(a) in favor of granting a leave to amend.”  Eminence Cap., 
22  316 F.3d at1052 (internal quotations omitted). Prejudice may exist where new allegations 
23  “greatly alter[] the nature of the litigation” and would require defendants to undertake, “at 
24  a late hour, an entirely new course of defense.” Morongo Band of Mission Indians v. 
25  Rose,
893 F.2d 1074, 1079
 (9th Cir. 1990); Peterson v. California, No. 1:10-cv-01132-
26  SMS,
2011 WL 3875622
, at *3 (E.D. Cal. Sept. 1, 2011) (“[W]hen, after a period of 
27  extensive discovery, a party proposes a late-tendered amendment that would 
28  fundamentally change the case to incorporate new causes of action and that would require 
1  additional discovery, the amendment may be appropriately denied as prejudicial to the 
2  opposing party.”).                                                        
3       Here, Defendants make no argument they will suffer from undue prejudice should 
4  Plaintiff’s Motion to Amend be granted, and as stated above, it is the non-movant’s 
5  burden to demonstrate prejudice. Plaintiff argues that he does “not add these parties or 
6  new claims late to litigation as the case was only filed in August of 2022.” ECF No. 16-1 
7  at 9.

9  unduly prejudice Defendants. The new claims and allegations do not alter the nature of 
10  the litigation to a significant extent as they all concern Defendant Brown’s allegedly 
11  improper and illegal actions. Further, the litigation is in early stages.  Plaintiff filed his 
12  Motion for Leave to Amend only four and a half months after filing of the initial 
13  Complaint. Defendants have filed Motions to Dismiss, but no significant briefing has 
14  occurred on the arguments presented therein. See Fremantlemedia N. Am., Inc. v. AXA 
15  Ins. Co.,
2010 WL 11601204
, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Nov. 5, 2010) (granting motion for leave 
16  to amend because the case was in “its early stages and neither party has conducted 
17  discovery, except for initial disclosures”). Accordingly, Defendant has not demonstrated 
18  it would be prejudiced by the filing of an amended complaint, and thus, this factor weighs 
19  in favor of granting leave to amend.                                      
20       D.   Futility                                                        
21       An amendment is futile “only if it would clearly be subject to dismissal.” SAES 
22  Getters,
219 F. Supp. 2d at 1086
 (citing DCD Programs, 83 F.2d at 188). Amendment is 
23  futile when a court could not “conceive of additional facts that could, if formally alleged, 
24  support the claim[s].” Corinthian Colls.,
655 F.3d at 995
. “While courts will determine 
25  the legal sufficiency of a proposed amendment using the same standard as applied on a 
26  Rule 12(b)(6) motion . . . such issues are often more appropriately raised in a motion to 
27  dismiss rather than in an opposition to a motion for leave to amend.” SAES Getters, 219 
28  F. Supp. 2d at 1086. Courts generally do not consider the validity of a proposed amended 
1 || pleading in deciding whether to grant leave to amend, instead deferring consideration of 
2    challenges to the merits after leave to amend is granted and the amended pleadings are 
3 || filed. See id.; Clarke v.  Upton,
703 F. Supp. 2d 1037, 1043
 (E.D. Cal. 2010) (“[D]enial 
4        a motion to amend] on this ground is rare and courts generally defer considerations of 
5 || challenges to the merits of a proposed amended pleading until after leave to amend is 
6 || granted and the amended pleading 1s filed.’’). 
7         Due to the complexity of the legal issues and sheer volume of factual allegations, 
8 || arguments, and Defendants, the Court finds Defendants’ arguments are more 
9 || appropriately resolved at the Motion to Dismiss stage after substantive briefing by all 
10 || Parties. Plaintiff has yet to respond to the Motions to Dismiss and was limited to the 
11    length of a Reply brief to respond to Defendants’ substantive arguments presented in 
12 || their Oppositions to the present Motion. Due to the complicated nature of the factual 
13 || allegations and causes of action, the Court is not prepared to say that there exists no 
14 || factual scenario in which all or some of Plaintiff's causes of action can survive a Motion 
15        Dismiss against all or some of the Defendants. 
16         Overall, the Foman factors weigh in favor of permitting Plaintiff to amend his 
17   ||Complaint. The Court GRANTS Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to File an Amended 
18   ||Complaint given the strong federal policy favoring amendments due to a preference for 
19 || resolving cases on the merits. See DCD Programs, Ltd.,
833 F.2d at 186
.

16       Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss argue that Plaintiff’s Complaint should be 
17  dismissed under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“Rule”) 12(b)(1) for lack of subject 
18  matter jurisdiction, Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim, and Rule 12(b)(7) for failure 
19  to join an indispensable party. Some Defendants also move under Rule 12(f) to strike 
20  portions of Plaintiff’s FAC.                                              
21    I.   Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1)                           
22       Rule 12(b)(1) permits dismissal of a claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. 
23  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1). Dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction should be 
24  granted if the complaint, considered in its entirety, fails to allege facts sufficient to 
25  establish subject matter jurisdiction. In re Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) 
26  Antitrust Litig., 546 F.3d 981, 984-85 (9th Cir. 2008). The Plaintiff bears the burden of 
27                                                                            
1  proving that a federal court has subject matter jurisdiction. Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 
2  U.S. 330, 338 (2016); see also McCauley v. Ford Motor Co., 264 F.3d 952, 957 (9th Cir. 
3  2001) (citing McNutt General Motors Acceptance Corp., 298 U.S. 178, 189 (1936)).  
4       A Rule 12(b)(1) attack may be facial or factual. Safe Air for Everyone v. Meyer, 
5  373 F.3d 1035, 1039 (9th Cir. 2004). In a facial attack, defendant asserts that the 
6  allegations in the complaint are insufficient to prove federal subject matter jurisdiction. 
7  Id. The court resolves a facial attack as a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss—the court 
8  accepts the factual allegations in the complaint as true and determines if the allegations 
9  are sufficient to properly invoke federal jurisdiction. Leite v. Crane Co., 749 F.3d 1117, 
10  1121 (9th Cir. 2014). In a factual attack, defendant disputes the very truth of the factual 
11  allegations themselves that are said to invoke subject matter jurisdiction. Safe Air for 
12  Everyone, 373 F.3d at 1039. To resolve a factual attack, the court is permitted to review 
13  evidence beyond the complaint. Id.                                        
14       Defendants do not appear to dispute the truthfulness of the underlying allegations, 
15  simply that they do not give rise to federal subject matter jurisdiction. Thus, this is a 
16  facial attack, and the Court will determine whether the allegations in Plaintiff’s 
17  Complaint, taken as true, sufficiently support a finding of subject matter jurisdiction. 
18    II.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6)                           
19       Rule 12(b)(6) permits dismissal for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be 
20  granted.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6). Rule 8(a)(2) states that a pleading must contain “a 
21  short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.” Fed. 
22  R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2). A plaintiff is not required to provide “detailed factual allegations,” but 
23  the plaintiff must plead sufficient facts that, if accepted as true, “raise a right to relief 
24  above the speculative level.” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 545 (2007). A 
25  complaint will survive a motion to dismiss when it contains enough facts to “state a claim 
26  to relief that is plausible on its face.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting 
27                                                                            
1  Twombly, 550 U.S. at 570). A claim is plausible when the factual allegations permit “the 
2  court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct 
3  charged.” Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678. Further, under Rule 9(b), when the complaint includes 
4  allegations of fraud, a party must “state with particularity the circumstances constituting 
5  fraud or mistake.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).                                 
6       The Court is not required to accept as true “allegations that are merely conclusory, 
7  unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” In re Gilead Scis. Sec. 
8  Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055 (9th Cir. 2008). “Threadbare recitals of the elements of a 
9  cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice.” Iqbal, 556 
10  U.S. at 678.                                                              
11    III.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(7)                          
12       Under Rule 12(b)(7), a defendant may move to dismiss for a failure to join a party 
13  under Rule 19. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(7). A Rule 19 motion poses three questions: (1) 
14  whether the nonparty should be joined under Rule 19(a); (2) if the nonparty is necessary 
15  under Rule 19(a), whether it is feasible to order the nonparty be joined; and (3) if joinder 
16  is not feasible, whether the case can proceed without the nonparty, or whether the 
17  nonparty is an “indispensable party” such that the action must be dismissed. Upper Deck 
18  Co. v. Flores, 569 F. Supp. 3d 1050, 1070 (S.D. Cal. 2021) (citing EEOC V. Peabody W. 
19  Coal Co., 400 F.3d 774, 779 (9th Cir. 2005)).                             
20    IV.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(f)                              
21       Rule 12(f) states that a court “may strike from a pleading an insufficient defense or 
22  any redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f). 
23  “The function of a 12(f) motion to strike is to avoid the expenditure of time and money 
24  that must arise from litigating spurious issues by dispensing with those issues prior to 
25  trial . . . .” Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 973 (9th Cir. 2010). 
26  “[M]otions to strike should not be granted unless it is clear that the matter to be stricken 
27                                                                            
1  could have no possible bearing on the subject matter of the litigation.” Colaprico v. Sun 
2  Microsys., Inc., 758 F. Supp. 1335, 1339 (N.D. Cal. 1991).

11            i.   18 U.S.C. § 1962(a)

13  received any income derived, directly or indirectly, from a pattern of racketeering activity

19  Cir. 1992). A plaintiff “must include allegations of injury from the use and investment of 
20  racketeering proceeds, not merely injury from the predicate acts of racketeering

7  pattern of racketeering activity . . . to acquire or maintain, directly or indirectly, any 
8  interest in or control of any enterprise which is engaged in, or the activities of which 
9  affect, interstate or foreign commerce.” § 1962(b) requires “a specific nexus between the 
10  control of the enterprise and the racketeering activity.” Sea-Land, 57 F. Supp. 2d at 1055. 
11  Plaintiff has not met this burden. Plaintiff has not pled facts showing that there is a nexus

3       To maintain a cause of action under RICO, a plaintiff must show not only that the 
4  defendant's violation was a “but for” cause of his injury, but that it was the proximate 
5  cause as well. Holmes v. Secs. Inv. Prot. Corp., 503 U.S. 258, 268 (1992)). This means 
6  there must be “some direct relation between the injury asserted and the injurious conduct 
7  alleged.” Id. Directness of the relationship is important for three reasons. “First, the less 
8  direct an injury is, the more difficult it becomes to ascertain the amount of a plaintiff's 
9  damages attributable to the violation, as distinct from other, independent, factors.” Id. at 
10  269-270. Second, courts would have to adopt complicated apportionment rules to avoid 
11  multiple recoveries. Id. Third, directly injured victims can generally be counted on to sue, 
12  “without any of the problems attendant upon suits by plaintiffs injured more remotely.” 
13  Id. (citing Associated Gen. Contractors of California, Inc. v. California State Council of 
14  Carpenters, 459 U.S. 519, 541–42 (1983)). These three policy concerns guide a court's 
15  evaluation of the directness of the injury under RICO. Id. at 270.

18       A. Citizenship                                                       
19       A person is a “citizen” of the state in which they are domiciled. Kantor v. 
20  Wellesley Galleries, Ltd., 704 F.2d 1088, 1090 (9th Cir. 1983). “A person’s domicile is 
21  [their] permanent home, where [they reside] with the intention to remain or to which 
22  [they] intend[] to return.” Kanter v. Warner-Lambert Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 
23  2001) (citing Lew v. Moss, 797 F.2d 747, 749 (9th Cir. 1986)). A person residing in a 
24  state is not necessary a citizen of that state. Id. An individual can reside in a state and be 
25  domiciled in another. Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30, 48 
26  (1989).

18 U.S.C. § 1962
(c), a plaintiff must allege the defendant participated in

23            iv.
18 U.S.C. § 1964
(c)                                        
24       RICO's provision for civil actions provides that “[a]ny person injured in his 
25  business or property by reason of a violation of section 1962 of this chapter may sue … 
26                                                                            
27                                                                            
1  and shall recover threefold the damages he sustains and the cost of the suit, including a 
2  reasonable attorney's fee.”
18 U.S.C. § 1964
(c).                          
3       To maintain a cause of action under RICO, a plaintiff must show not only that the 
4  defendant's violation was a “but for” cause of his injury, but that it was the proximate 
5  cause as well. Holmes v. Secs. Inv. Prot. Corp.,
503 U.S. 258, 268
 (1992)). This means 
6  there must be “some direct relation between the injury asserted and the injurious conduct 
7  alleged.”
Id.
 Directness of the relationship is important for three reasons. “First, the less 
8  direct an injury is, the more difficult it becomes to ascertain the amount of a plaintiff's 
9  damages attributable to the violation, as distinct from other, independent, factors.”
Id.
 at 
10  269-270. Second, courts would have to adopt complicated apportionment rules to avoid 
11  multiple recoveries.
Id.
 Third, directly injured victims can generally be counted on to sue, 
12  “without any of the problems attendant upon suits by plaintiffs injured more remotely.” 
13
Id.
 (citing Associated Gen. Contractors of California, Inc. v. California State Council of 
14  Carpenters,
459 U.S. 519
, 541–42 (1983)). These three policy concerns guide a court's 
15  evaluation of the directness of the injury under RICO. Id. at 270.        
16       At its core, the case involves Federal Excise Tax that was allegedly collected by 
17  JGH from clients but not remitted to the IRS as required by law. Compl. ⁋ 1.  From there, 
18  it is difficult to follow what Plaintiff alleges is his precise RICO injury, but the Court 
19  makes out the following allegations of injury and finds each defective in turn. See Compl. 
20  ⁋⁋ 103-104. First, Plaintiff states he “suffered injury derivatively to his reputation and 
21  business.” Compl. ⁋ 103. He states that his interests as a shareholder have been damaged 
22  due to the fraudulently charged FET. Id. However, shareholders do not generally have 
23  standing to assert RICO claims in an individual capacity. Ahn v. Hanil Dev. Inc., 2010
24 WL 11520673
, at *2 (C.D. Cal. Jan. 21, 2010); see also, Gaff v. Fed. Deposit Ins. Corp., 
25
814 F.2d 311, 315
 (6th Cir.), on reh'g in part,
828 F.2d 1145, 1147-48
 (6th Cir. 1987) 
26  (finding that as a general precept of corporate law a shareholder of a corporation does not 
27                                                                            
1  have a personal or individual right of action for damages based solely on an injury to the 
2  corporation). A shareholder “must show either an injury distinct from that to other 
3  shareholders or a special duty between [the defendants and the shareholder] if they are to 
4  having standing to assert RICO claims based on injury to the corporation.” Sparling v. 
5  Hoffman Const. Co., Inc.,
864 F.2d 635, 640
 (9th Cir. 1988). Plaintiff has shown neither. 
6  Any injury to his interests as a shareholder resulting from the collected and unremitted 
7  FET is not distinct from that of any other shareholder. Any “derivative[ injury to] his 
8  reputation and business” is just that—derivative—and does not meet the direct, proximate 
9  cause standard required under civil RICO. Further, Plaintiff has not pled that the 
10  Defendants owed him a special duty.                                       
11       Second, Plaintiff states he has suffered injury as a result of Defendants’ use of his 
12  intellectual property to commit criminal acts, and that the use of his intellectual property 
13  in the commission of crimes has damaged the value of his property. Compl. ⁋ 103. For 
14  the reasons discussed below, the Court finds that Plaintiff has not pled with particularity 
15  the substance of his intellectual property, and thus this cannot establish a legitimate injury 
16  under § 1962(c). Further, to prevail on his misappropriation of IP theory, Plaintiff will be 
17  required to demonstrate that his assignment of IP to JGH was obtained through fraud. 
18  This additional inquiry means any injury to Plaintiff resulting from the misappropriation 
19  of IP is “too remote” to form direct injury because the link between the failure to pay 
20  FET and harm to Plaintiffs’ IP is “purely contingent” on whether he was fraudulently 
21  induced to relinquish his rights. Holmes,
503 U.S. at 271
.  As the Holmes Court observed: 
22  “quite apart from problems of proving factual causation, recognizing claims of the 
23  indirectly injured would force courts to adopt complicated rules apportioning damages 
24  among plaintiffs removed at different levels of injury from the violative acts, to obviate 
25  the risk of multiple recoveries.” Holmes,
503 U.S. at 269
.                
26                                                                            
27                                                                            
1       Third, Plaintiff states he has suffered injury as a result of the $1.3 million that has 
2  been personally assessed against him by the IRS. Compl. ⁋ 104. Proximate cause analysis 
3  under civil RICO looks to who is the direct victim of the allegedly wrongful conduct. In 
4  Anza v. Ideal Steel Supply Corp.,
547 U.S. 451

5  pled proximate cause because the plaintiff was not the “direct victim of th[e] conduct”;

547 U.S. 451, 458

559 U.S. 1

9  company that sold cigarettes online because they failed to file information with the State 
10  of New York which would have allowed the City of New York to collect tax revenue on 
11  cigarettes sold out of the state. The Court in Hemi Group held that the City of New 
12  York’s purported injury by way of lost tax revenue was not direct enough to constitute 
13  proximate cause under civil RICO because the more direct victim was the State of New 
14  York; the State of New York was first in the chain of alleged victims. Hemi Group, LLC 
15  v. City of New York, N.Y.,
559 U.S. 1, 10-12
 (2010). The Court further reasoned that the 
16  State of New York was a better situated plaintiff and had incentive to sue defendant Hemi 
17  Group because the State of New York had also lost out on tax revenue.
Id. at 11-12
.

26 U.S.C. § 4281

22  contends that the CFG Enterprise used the wires to charge customers the FET falsely

26  for Defendants’ failure to remit the tax to the IRS.                      
27

2  direct victim of any purported RICO scheme. His alleged injury is premised on an

Id. at 268
. Here, Plaintiff is seeking treble damages for amounts owed 
11  by JGH customers to the IRS based on a convoluted set of facts that, at best, were

6  Cancer and Blood Disorder Treatment Inst.,
603 F. Supp. 3d 799
, 800 (D. Ariz. May 16, 
7  2022). Courts in this Circuit routinely find that although a plaintiff does not need to

10  knowledge in the trade or of special persons who are skilled in the trade, and to permit 
11  the defendant to ascertain at least the boundaries within which the secret lies.’” AlterG, 
12  Inc. v. Boost Treadmills LLC,
388 F. Supp. 3d 1133, 1144

13  Devices, Inc. v. LG Elecs., Inc.,
343 F. Supp. 3d 868, 881

17  customer lists and customer related information, pricing information, vendor lists and

23 Mar. 23
, 2018); see also AlterG,
388 F. Supp. 3d at 1145
 (citing Vendavo). Trade secrets 
24  defined in these “broad, categorical terms” which are “more descriptive of the types of

12       Because the Court has dismissed both of Plaintiff’s federal causes of action, 
13  subject matter jurisdiction cannot exist under
28 U.S.C. § 1331
. The Parties dispute 
14  whether diversity of citizenship exists to establish diversity jurisdiction under
28 U.S.C. § 15
  1332.
28 U.S.C. § 1332
(a) requires that (1) the amount in controversy exceed $75,000, 
16  and (2) the action is between citizens of different states. The Court finds there is not 
17  diversity of citizenship.                                                 
18       A. Citizenship                                                       
19       A person is a “citizen” of the state in which they are domiciled. Kantor v. 
20  Wellesley Galleries, Ltd.,
704 F.2d 1088, 1090
 (9th Cir. 1983). “A person’s domicile is 
21  [their] permanent home, where [they reside] with the intention to remain or to which 
22  [they] intend[] to return.” Kanter v. Warner-Lambert Co.,
265 F.3d 853, 857
 (9th Cir. 
23  2001) (citing Lew v. Moss,
797 F.2d 747, 749
 (9th Cir. 1986)). A person residing in a 
24  state is not necessary a citizen of that state.
Id.
 An individual can reside in a state and be 
25  domiciled in another. Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield,
490 U.S. 30
, 48 
26  (1989).                                                                   
27                                                                            
1       To determine domicile, a court should analyze a number of factors, including the 
2  person’s “current residence, voting registration and voting practices, location of personal 
3  and real property, location of brokerage and bank accounts, location of spouse and 
4  family, membership in unions and other organizations, place of employment or business, 
5  driver’s license and automobile registration, and payment of taxes.” Lew,
797 F.2d at 6
  750. A person’s old domicile is not relinquished until a new domicile is established.
Id.
 
7  “A change in domicile requires the confluence of (a) physical presence at the new 
8  location with (b) an intention to remain there indefinitely.”
Id.
 Diversity of citizenship is 
9  determined at the time the lawsuit is filed. Grupo Dataflux v. Alas Global Group, L.P., 
10
541 U.S. 567, 570-71

   FAC ⁋ 8.

   Kansas at the time he filed his lawsuit. As stated, “residence” is not enough to establish 
23                                                                            
   citizenship. Plaintiff would retain his California citizenship until he established his 
24                                                                            
   domicile in Kansas, and obtaining a leasehold and becoming a “resident” of the state does 
25

26                                                                            
   Plaintiff argues that “[a]fter commencing the underlying action, the IRS transferred [sic] 
27

2  to properly maintain his valid Kansas citizenship.” ECF No. 41 at 8 (citing FAC ⁋ 62). He 
3  also states he received mail from Defendants at his address in Kansas.
Id.
  
4       Plaintiff’s bears the burden of proving to this Court that subject matter jurisdiction 
5  exists, and his argument does not establish he was a citizen of Kansas at the time his 
6  lawsuit was filed. See Grupo Dataflux,
541 U.S. at 570-71
. Indeed, the evidence he 
7  provides to support his assertion is an event that occurred after the lawsuit was filed (his

9  simply receiving mail in Kansas, from Defendants or anyone else for that matter, is not 
10  enough for the Court to determine that Plaintiff had established a residence and developed 
11  an intent to remain in Kansas. Because Plaintiff remains a citizen of California until he 
12  establishes domicile in another state, the Court finds Plaintiff has not shown he was not a 
13  citizen of California when he filed the initial Complaint. Because at least one of the 
14  Defendants (JGH) is a citizen of California, diversity jurisdiction does not exist, and the 
15  Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over Plaintiff’s action. Accordingly, Plaintiff’s 
16  remaining state law claims must be DISMISSED.

11  II.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                      
12       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b), a party is entitled to seek discovery of 
13  “any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional 
14  to the needs of the case, considering the importance of the issues at stake in the action, the 
15  amount in controversy, the parties’ relative access to relevant information, the parties’ 
16  resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving the issues, and whether the burden 
17  or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
18  26(b)(1).  Information need not be admissible to be discoverable.  Id.    
19       “The party seeking to compel discovery has the burden of establishing that its request 
20  satisfies the relevancy requirements of Rule 26(b)(1).”  Alves v. Riverside Cnty., 339 F.R.D. 
21  556, 559 (C.D. Cal. 2021) (quoting Bryant v. Ochoa, No. 07-CV-00200-JM-PCL, 2009 
22  WL 1390794, at *1 (S.D. Cal. May 14, 2009)).  “District courts have broad discretion in 
23  determining relevancy for discovery purposes.”  Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Prods., 
24  406 F.3d 625, 635 (9th Cir. 2005) (citing Hallett v. Morgan, 296 F.3d 732, 751 (9th Cir. 
25  2002)).    “Once  the  propounding  party  establishes  that  the  request  seeks  relevant 
26  information, ‘[t]he party who resists discovery has the burden to show discovery should 
27  not  be  allowed,  and  has  the  burden  of  clarifying,  explaining,  and  supporting  its 
28  objections.’”  Goro v. Flowers Foods, Inc., 334 F.R.D. 275, 283 (S.D. Cal. 2018) (quoting 
1  Superior Commc’ns v. Earhugger, Inc., 257 F.R.D. 215, 217 (C.D. Cal. 2009)).  However, 
2  a court must—either on motion or sua sponte—”limit the frequency or extent” of otherwise 
3  permissible discovery if the court finds, inter alia, the request “unreasonably cumulative 
4  or  duplicative”  or  the  discovery  sought  is  obtainable  from  a  “more  convenient,  less 
5  burdensome, or less expensive” source.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(C)(i).

12       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b), a party is entitled to seek discovery of 
13  “any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional 
14  to the needs of the case, considering the importance of the issues at stake in the action, the 
15  amount in controversy, the parties’ relative access to relevant information, the parties’ 
16  resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving the issues, and whether the burden 
17  or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
18  26(b)(1).  Information need not be admissible to be discoverable.  Id.    
19       “The party seeking to compel discovery has the burden of establishing that its request 
20  satisfies the relevancy requirements of Rule 26(b)(1).”  Alves v. Riverside Cnty.,
339 F.R.D. 21
  556, 559 (C.D. Cal. 2021) (quoting Bryant v. Ochoa, No. 07-CV-00200-JM-PCL, 2009
22 WL 1390794
, at *1 (S.D. Cal. May 14, 2009)).  “District courts have broad discretion in 
23  determining relevancy for discovery purposes.”  Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Prods., 
24
406 F.3d 625, 635
 (9th Cir. 2005) (citing Hallett v. Morgan,
296 F.3d 732
, 751 (9th Cir.

26  information, ‘[t]he party who resists discovery has the burden to show discovery should 
27  not  be  allowed,  and  has  the  burden  of  clarifying,  explaining,  and  supporting  its 
28  objections.’”  Goro v. Flowers Foods, Inc.,
334 F.R.D. 275

257 F.R.D. 215, 217
